earlier_scan.source_named: Glottolog sources for chig1239 are comparative/classification only (Josserand 1983, Auderset et al. 2023, Smith-Stark); no grammar or phonology of Chigmecatitlan Mixtec located.

new_statements.quote: en caso del Mixteco y sus variantes, es difícil ya que se rigen por las entonaciones de las palabras, por ejemplo, en el da´an davi decir sal o granizo se utilizan las consonantes i,i,n, pero la diferencia está en su pronunciación por tonos: Sal: “i in” Granizo: “ii n” Tan solo hacer uso de la escritura es difícil para comprender la variación de estas dos palabras
new_statements.translation: in the case of Mixtec and its variants it is difficult, since they are governed by the intonations of the words; for example, in da'an davi, to say 'salt' or 'hail' the [letters] i, i, n are used, but the difference lies in their pronunciation by tones: Salt: 'i in' / Hail: 'ii n'. Using writing alone makes it hard to grasp the variation between these two words
new_statements.citation: Telesforo Escamilla, Isabel. 2019. El proceso de enseñanza-aprendizaje de la lengua da'an davi en las mujeres adultas de Santa Catarina Tlaltempan. Tesis de licenciatura en Pedagogía, Facultad de Estudios Superiores Aragón, Universidad Nacional Autónoma de México, 121 pp.
new_statements.locator: Conclusiones, printed p. 113 (p. 115); identity passage p. 66 (p. 68); interview remark 'habla como… da un tono diferente, como los de Santa María' p. 96 (p. 98)
new_statements.relation_note: A lay, variety-specific assertion that Tlaltempan Mixtec distinguishes words by tone, illustrated with one (orthographically crude, tone-unmarked) minimal pair 'salt' vs 'hail'; also states (p. 66) that the variety has no written tradition and 'no existen registros algunos sobre su alfabeto que puedan mostrar la estructura lingüística de la misma'. Nothing on word stress/acento (the word 'acento' occurs only about Spanish spelling lessons). No tone inventory, no analysis.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Lexical tone contrast asserted for Tlaltempan da'an davi (sal vs granizo differ only 'por tonos'); no stress statement.
new_statements.identity_note: About the Mixtec of Santa Catarina Tlaltempan, Puebla ('da'an davi (de Tlaltempan)', INALI 'mixteco del suroeste de Puebla', IPA [ðãʔã ðaβi], p. 66), one of the two chig1239 [mii] towns; author is from the community; contrasts it with the speech of Chigmecatitlán and Zacapala (p. 66) and 'los de Santa María' (interview, p. 96). Pedagogy/sociolinguistics (language workshops with adult women), not a linguistic description. | Same author and variety: 'mixteco de Tlaltempan o como se autodenominan da'an davi o de'e dau de Tlaltempan' (p. 68), migrants from Santa Catarina Tlaltempan in Mexico City; mentions 'mixteco de Chigmecatitlán o dehe dau' (p. 132) as the neighbouring variety; reproduces Josserand 1983's dialect-area map (p. 67). Title spells the autonym with grave (low-tone) accents, unexplained in the text. Language-ideology study, not a description.

new_statements.quote: Las lenguas mixtecas son consideradas tonales, puede que estas se escriban igual, pero la forma de decirlo cambia por completo el significado del mismo (Telesforo, 2019): Sal: “i in” Granizo: “ii n” Esto ha sido fundamental para poder identificar una variante de otra
new_statements.translation: The Mixtec languages are considered tonal; they may be written the same, but the way of saying it completely changes the meaning (Telesforo 2019): Salt 'i in' / Hail 'ii n'. This has been fundamental for telling one variant from another

new_statements.quote: CGM: Ordaz Peregrina, Nazario Ignacio, Vicente Jerónimo Palacios Mexicano and Martiniano Beltrán Méndez, native speakers of Chigmecatitlán Mixtec. Don Nazario was born in 1927, don Vicente in 1928, and Martiniano in 1960. They were interviewed by Sebastian van Doesburg, Michael W. Swanton and A. de Ávila on July 25, 2009, in Santa María Chigmecatitlán. Historical narrative, grammatical paradigms, place names and plant lexicon were recorded digitally and transcribed. Swanton is studying the phonological traits of this Mixtec variant, including underlying tones and sandhi rules; surface tones have been marked tentatively, pending further analysis.
new_statements.citation: de Avila [Blomberg], Alejandro. 2010. Mixtec plant nomenclature and classification. PhD dissertation (Anthropology), University of California, Berkeley. 273 pp.
new_statements.locator: ch. 3, list of sources by community code, entry 'CGM', printed p. 77 (p. 86; extracted text); tone-marking convention sec. 3.2 'Mixtec orthography' printed p. 50 (p. 59); /dz/ remark p. 50; CGM forms e.g. p. 88 'yutnú: árbol (CGM)', p. 135 'yukú / kú: yerba (CGM)' vs 'yuku: hoja (CGM)'; note [9.] p. 229; reference 'Ordaz Peregrina et al. 2009' p. 257
new_statements.relation_note: Variety-specific, first-hand but preliminary: the 2009 Chigmecatitlan recordings were transcribed with SURFACE TONES marked tentatively (three-level low/mid/high convention of the Mixtec Academy, p. 50: 'I underline low-tone vowels, mark high tone with acute accents and leave the mid-tone unmarked'), and Swanton 'is studying the phonological traits of this Mixtec variant, including underlying tones and sandhi rules'. The CGM forms in the plant lists carry these marks (15 of ~85 CGM headwords show an acute, almost always on the final vowel: yutnu-H 'arbol', tnudichi-H 'biznaga', tnunima-H 'cazahuate', yuku-H 'yerba' vs yuku 'hoja'). No tone inventory is asserted beyond the tentative three-le…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Chigmecatitlan Mixtec is treated as a tone language: surface tones transcribed tentatively on a low / mid / high scale (acute = high, underline = low, mid unmarked); underlying tones and tone sandhi under study (Swanton), no analysis published; nothing on word stress.
new_statements.exceptions: none; marking explicitly 'tentative, pending further analysis'
new_statements.identity_note: Ethnobotanical-linguistic dissertation covering ~40 Mixtec varieties; source code 'CGM: Santa Maria Chigmecatitlan, district of Tepexi de Rodriguez, Puebla: 1507 m asl' (p. 74) and 'CGM: Chigmecatitlan - NORTHERN BAJA - Chigmecatitlan Mixtec - mixteco del suroeste de Puebla' (p. 86) = exactly chig1239 (Ethnologue name + INALI name); the CGM material is FIRST-HAND: three named native speakers (b. 1927, 1928, 1960) recorded in Santa Maria Chigmecatitlan on 25 July 2009 by Sebastian van Doesburg, Michael W. Swanton and the author (historical narrative, grammatical paradigms, place names, plant lexicon), cited as Ordaz Peregrina et al. 2009. About 85 CGM lexical entries appear in chs. 4-5 in the Ve'e Tu'un Savi orthography with surface tones (acute = high, underline = low, unmarked = mid; underlining is lost in extracted text), e.g. p. 135 'yuku / ku [acute on final u]: yerba (CGM)' vs 'yuku: hoja (CGM)'; segmental notes: /dz/ in Chigmecatitlan Mixtec (p. 50), *tV~ > tnV~ innovation confirmed there (note 9, p. 229), genitive x-NOUN (p. 135). Tlaltempan appears only as Josserand's 'Tlaltempan sub-area' of Northern Baja (pp. 17, 85), no data.

sources.note: Autonym Da'an davi; Tlaltempan + Chigmecatitlán; 1,350 (2010 INEGI); 'None known. 23% intelligibility of Chazumba.. Low intelligibility with all Mixtec; very different.' Latin script; no literature. Nothing on stress.

sources.citation: Old SIL Mexico site, Mixtecan family index page (the Internet Archive 2007-10-26)
sources.note: Links to ~15 SIL-studied Mixtec varieties (Alacatlatzala, Magdalena Peñasco, Mixtepec, Tezoatlán, Xochapa, Yosondúa..); no Chigmecatitlán page exists. General remark that Mixtecan languages are tonal; nothing on stress.

sources.citation: Ochoa Cabrera, José Antonio. 1993. Las bandas de viento en la vida de los mixtecos de Santa María Chigmecatitlán: análisis de la función social de las bandas de música mixtecas. Tesis de licenciatura en Etnología, Escuela Nacional de Antropología e Historia, México, 305 pp.
sources.note: Lay remark on segmental sounds (no f, glottal stop 'saltillo'), speaker census (64% bilingual, 15% Mixtec monolingual), note that Chigmecatitlán and Tlaltempan speech differ enough to hinder communication; nothing on tone or stress. Only contents pages and pp. 39-40 scanned (scanned PDF, page cap).

sources.citation: Bradley, C. Henry & J. Kathryn Josserand (dirs.), CIS-INAH Programa de Lingüística, Proyecto Mixteco. 1977-1979. 'Reconocimiento del mixteco' / 'Cuestionario de sintaxis' dialect-survey questionnaires (ca. 170 towns), ms. transcriptions with tone/stress marks. Archived as 'Mixtec Languages Collection of Kathryn Josserand' (AILLA, UT Austin); crowd-transcribed as 'The Kathryn Josserand Mixtec Language Surveys' (FromThePage, UT Libraries).
sources.note: marks only: Tlaltempan items 1-20, 26-30, 41-45, 91-95 transcribed with stress ticks ('njika 'njii 'sol', 'šio 'luna', 'kimi~ 'estrella', 'dabi 'lluvia'); Chigmecatitlán toponyms with ticks ('ñukoʔyo México, 'ñuu 'kaba Tepexi); no tone digits, no statement.

sources.note: no phonology content -- historical demography from the parish archive (1770-1954), settlement, economy (palm weaving, sweets); confirms unpublished INAH linguistic field notes on the variety exist (Manrique 1957).

sources.citation: Arana Osnaya, Evangelina. 1960. Relaciones internas del mixteco-trique. Anales del Instituto Nacional de Antropología e Historia (sexta época) tomo XII, núm. 41 (1959): 219-273. México: INAH/SEP.
sources.note: Comparative phonology and lexicostatistics of the four Mixtecan divisions with Chigmecatitlán/Tlaltempan reflexes cited without tone marks. Prosody p. 232 (p. 242): tone deliberately NOT treated ('En el presente estudio no se ha tomado en cuenta el tono por falta de datos adecuados.. no se indica el tono aun cuando probablemente todos los dialectos lo tienen'); accent reconstructed for the proto-language on the root, penultimate root syllable in Cuicatec and Mixtec vs final in Trique/Amuzgo, and 'Actualmente, el mixteco tiene el acento en la posición referida, según observaciones hechas perso…

sources.citation: Mak, Cornelia & Robert E. Longacre. 1960. Proto-Mixtec Phonology. International Journal of American Linguistics 26(1): 23-40
sources.note: SIL tags Chigmecatitlán Mixtec [mii] as a subject language; the paper compares the phonologies of 22 Mixtec variants and may note stress/couplet structure for the Chigmecatitlán data set.

sources.citation: Swadesh, Morris. 1960. The Oto-Manguean Hypothesis and Macro Mixtecan. International Journal of American Linguistics 26(2): 79-111.
sources.note: Long-range comparative etymologies; Chigmecatitlán appears only as two lexical citations without tone marks; general discussion of Macro-Mixtecan root accent, nothing variety-specific. Wordlist-level data only.

sources.citation: Arana Osnaya, Evangelina. 1957. Relaciones internas del tronco mixteco. Tesis profesional (Maestría en Ciencias Antropológicas, Lingüística), Escuela Nacional de Antropología e Historia, México, 66 pp. (dir. Mauricio Swadesh; INAH repository record dated 1997, catalogue X4A1957A73r).
sources.note: Comparative/lexicostatistic thesis; phonology chapter reconstructs proto-Mixtecan segments; tone not treated for lack of data; generic remarks that probably all Mixtec dialects are tonal and that root accent is penultimate in 'some Mixtec dialects' the author observed (she worked on coast dialects) -- nothing specific to the Chigmecatitlán/Tlaltempan lists, which appear untoned. Establishes that L. Manrique (ENAH/INAH) collected Chigmecatitlán and Tlaltempan wordlists in Jan 1957. Remaining pp. 25-84 (consonant/vowel developments, lexicostatistic tables, diagnostic list) not scanned (page cap…
